title: Two-Carbonate Mixture by Mass Loss
setup: A 2.00 g mixture of CaCO₃ (M = 100.09 g/mol) and MgCO₃ (M = 84.31 g/mol) is heated strongly until both decompose completely to metal oxides and CO₂(g) (M = 44.01 g/mol). The sample loses 0.940 g of mass. Find the mass percent of CaCO₃ in the original mixture.
strategy: Bound the answer with pure-component limits before setting up simultaneous equations.

steps.say: If the 2.00 g sample were pure CaCO₃, what percent of its mass would escape as CO₂?
steps.hint: One mole of CaCO₃ (100.09 g) releases one mole of CO₂ (44.01 g).
steps.explain: 44.01 / 100.09 × 100 = 43.97%, about 44.0% mass loss for pure CaCO₃.

steps.say: If the sample were pure MgCO₃ instead, what percent of its mass would escape as CO₂?
steps.hint: One mole of MgCO₃ (84.31 g) also releases one mole of CO₂ (44.01 g).
steps.explain: 44.01 / 84.31 × 100 = 52.20%. Lighter cation means a larger fraction of the mass is CO₂.

steps.say: The actual mass loss is 0.940 g out of 2.00 g (47.0%). Before solving, which carbonate makes up more of the mixture by mass?

options.label: CaCO₃, because 47.0% is closer to 44.0% than to 52.2%
MgCO₃, because 47.0% is closer to 52.2% than to 44.0%
Equal masses of both, because 47.0% is the exact midpoint
Cannot tell without knowing the temperature

steps.hint: Compare the gap from 47.0% to 44.0% against the gap from 47.0% to 52.2%.
steps.explain: 47.0% sits 3.0 points above CaCO₃ (44.0%) and 5.2 points below MgCO₃ (52.2%), so CaCO₃ must be slightly over 60% by mass.

steps.say: How many total moles of CO₂ escaped? (This equals n(CaCO₃) + n(MgCO₃).)
steps.hint: Divide the lost mass of CO₂ by 44.01 g/mol.
steps.explain: 0.940 g / 44.01 g/mol = 0.02136 mol CO₂, so n(CaCO₃) + n(MgCO₃) = 0.02136 mol.

steps.say: Let x = n(CaCO₃), so n(MgCO₃) = 0.02136 − x. Using 100.09x + 84.31(0.02136 − x) = 2.00, what is x?
steps.hint: Expand 84.31 × 0.02136 = 1.801 g, subtract from 2.00 g, and divide by (100.09 − 84.31) = 15.78 g/mol.

steps.say: What is the mass percent of CaCO₃ in the 2.00 g mixture?
steps.hint: Convert x to grams of CaCO₃ (× 100.09), divide by 2.00 g, and multiply by 100.
steps.explain: 0.01262 mol × 100.09 g/mol = 1.263 g CaCO₃, which is 63.2% — matching our bound estimate.

finish: Bounding a mixture between its two pure extremes predicts the answer before you write an equation and catches algebra slips instantly.
takeaway: For any two-component mixture, compute the pure-A and pure-B endpoints first; the observed value's lever-arm position between them gives the composition.

title: Photon Flux and Beer–Lambert Dilution
setup: A 520 nm laser delivers 0.250 W (0.250 J/s) into a dye solution for 60.0 s. Separately, the stock dye is too concentrated to measure directly, so 5.00 mL is diluted to 25.00 mL; the diluted sample has absorbance A = 0.240 in a 1.00 cm cell (ε = 4.80 × 10⁴ M⁻¹·cm⁻¹). Find the moles of photons delivered and the stock dye concentration.
strategy: Chain units from macroscopic power (J/s) down to one photon (hc/λ), and treat dilution as a pure scale factor on concentration.

steps.say: How many joules of light energy enter the cell in 60.0 s?
steps.hint: Power in watts is joules per second: E_total = P × t.

steps.say: What is the energy of a single 520 nm photon? (h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, c = 2.998 × 10⁸ m/s)
steps.hint: Convert 520 nm to 520 × 10⁻⁹ m, then use E = hc / λ.

steps.say: How many moles of photons hit the cell in 60.0 s? (N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
steps.hint: Divide total energy by energy per photon to get photon count, then divide by N_A.
steps.explain: 15.0 J / (3.82 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) = 3.93 × 10¹⁹ photons; dividing by 6.022 × 10²³ gives 6.52 × 10⁻⁵ mol photons.

steps.say: Why must a very dark stock solution (A > 1.5) be diluted before measuring on a spectrophotometer?

options.label: Very little light reaches the detector, so stray light breaks linearity between A and c
The molar absorptivity ε becomes zero at high concentration
Dilution changes the wavelength of maximum absorption
Beer's law only applies when A < 0.01

steps.hint: At A = 2, only 1% of incident light transmits; any small detector noise or stray light dominates.
steps.explain: At high absorbance almost no light reaches the detector, so tiny stray-light errors distort A; diluting brings A into the reliable ~0.1–1.0 window.

steps.say: What is the concentration of the diluted dye solution from A = εbc?
Since 5.00 mL of stock was diluted to 25.00 mL, what was the stock concentration?
steps.hint: Moles of dye are conserved: c_stock = c_dil × (25.00 / 5.00).
steps.explain: A 5-fold dilution means the stock is 5× more concentrated: 5 × 5.00 × 10⁻⁶ = 2.50 × 10⁻⁵ M.

finish: Light energy bridges watts to moles through E = hc/λ and N_A, while Beer–Lambert readings scale straight back through the dilution factor.
takeaway: Always check the measurement window (A around 0.1–1.0) and undo dilutions by multiplying by V_final / V_aliquot.

title: Predicting Lattice Energy by Ratio Scaling
setup: NaCl, CaS, and MgO all crystallize in the exact same rock-salt lattice. NaCl has lattice energy 787 kJ/mol and interionic distance d = 282 pm. CaS has d = 284 pm, and MgO has d = 210 pm. Estimate the lattice energies of CaS and MgO using Coulomb scaling U ∝ |q₁q₂| / d.
strategy: Take ratios against a known compound with the same crystal geometry so all geometric constants cancel out.

steps.say: Why does dividing U(MgO) by U(NaCl) eliminate the crystal-structure constant (Madelung constant)?

options.label: Both share the same rock-salt geometry, so the same constant sits in numerator and denominator
The constant is always equal to 1
Lattice energy does not depend on crystal geometry
Charges cancel the geometry factor

steps.hint: When two crystals have the same arrangement of ions, their proportionality constant k is identical.
steps.explain: Because U = k|q₁q₂|/d with the same rock-salt constant k, taking a ratio cancels k cleanly.

steps.say: What is the charge-product ratio |q₁q₂|(CaS) / |q₁q₂|(NaCl)?
steps.hint: Ca²⁺ and S²⁻ have charges 2 and 2; Na⁺ and Cl⁻ have charges 1 and 1.
steps.explain: (2 × 2) / (1 × 1) = 4. Doubling both ion charges quadruples the electrostatic attraction.

steps.say: Using U(CaS) ≈ U(NaCl) × 4 × (d_NaCl / d_CaS), estimate the lattice energy of CaS.
steps.hint: Multiply 787 by 4 and by 282 / 284.
steps.explain: 787 × 4 × (282 / 284) = 3126 kJ/mol (experimental value is ~3060 kJ/mol — within 2%!).

steps.say: Now estimate the lattice energy of MgO (charges ±2, d = 210 pm) by scaling from NaCl.
steps.hint: Multiply 787 by 4 (charge ratio) and by 282 / 210 (inverse distance ratio).
steps.explain: 787 × 4 × (282 / 210) = 4227 kJ/mol (actual is ~3850 kJ/mol; short-range repulsion trims the pure point-charge estimate by ~9%).

steps.say: Between CaS and MgO, which factor accounts for MgO's higher melting point?

options.label: Smaller interionic distance d (210 pm vs 284 pm), since both have ±2 charges
Higher ion charges in MgO than in CaS
Larger molar mass of MgO
Stronger dispersion forces in MgO

steps.hint: Both compounds are 2+/2−; only the ion separation changes.
steps.explain: With identical ±2 charges, Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ sit much closer (210 pm vs 284 pm), making MgO's lattice ~35% harder to break apart.

finish: Ratio scaling turns a qualitative trend (higher charge, smaller radius) into a quantitative estimate without memorizing lattice constants.
takeaway: Whenever a physical law has an unknown constant (U ∝ q₁q₂/d, PV = nRT, rate ∝ [A]^m), divide the target case by a reference case to cancel the constant.

title: Two Bulbs and a Gas-to-Solid Reaction
setup: Bulb A (2.00 L) holds NH₃(g) at 1.50 atm. Bulb B (3.00 L) holds HCl(g) at 0.800 atm. Both are at 298 K. A stopcock connecting them opens, and NH₃(g) + HCl(g) → NH₄Cl(s) runs to completion at 298 K. Find the final pressure in the connected bulbs.
strategy: At constant T, PV is directly proportional to moles — do the entire stoichiometry in L·atm without ever touching R or T.

steps.say: Why can we track moles of gas using the product PV (in L·atm) instead of computing n = PV/(RT)?

options.label: RT is the same for every gas at 298 K, so PV is strictly proportional to n
R equals 1 at 298 K
Pressure is conserved when gases react
Volume does not affect gas moles

steps.hint: Look at n = PV / (RT): if T never changes, RT is just a constant scaling factor.
steps.explain: Because RT is constant throughout, multiplying and dividing by RT would only cancel at the end.

steps.say: Compute P·V for NH₃(g) in Bulb A.
steps.hint: Multiply 1.50 atm by 2.00 L.

steps.say: Compute P·V for HCl(g) in Bulb B.
steps.hint: Multiply 0.800 atm by 3.00 L.

steps.say: Which gas is left over after the 1:1 reaction to solid NH₄Cl finishes?

options.label: NH₃(g), because 3.00 L·atm > 2.40 L·atm
HCl(g), because Bulb B has the larger volume
Neither, because both react completely
NH₄Cl(g), because a new gas forms

steps.hint: Compare the mole proxies (PV): 3.00 L·atm of NH₃ vs 2.40 L·atm of HCl.
steps.explain: All 2.40 L·atm of HCl reacts with 2.40 L·atm of NH₃, leaving 0.60 L·atm of NH₃(g) and solid NH₄Cl (negligible volume).

steps.say: The remaining 0.60 L·atm of NH₃(g) fills both bulbs (total volume 5.00 L). What is the final pressure?
steps.hint: Divide the leftover PV (0.60 L·atm) by the total volume (2.00 + 3.00 = 5.00 L).
steps.explain: P_final = 0.60 L·atm / 5.00 L = 0.120 atm.

finish: Working in PV units at constant T cuts out two unnecessary conversions through RT and makes limiting-reactant gas problems effortless.
takeaway: At constant temperature, PV is a direct currency for gas moles: add or subtract PV values, then divide by total volume.

title: Calorimetry with Cup Heat Capacity and Excess Acid
setup: 50.0 mL of 1.20 M HCl and 50.0 mL of 0.800 M NaOH (both at 22.0 °C) are mixed in a calorimeter whose heat capacity is C_cal = 25.0 J/°C. The temperature rises to 27.1 °C. Assume solution density 1.00 g/mL and specific heat 4.184 J/(g·°C). Find ΔH_rxn in kJ per mole of H₂O formed.
strategy: Account for every heat sink (both the full 100 g solution and the calorimeter body), then divide by moles of the limiting reactant only.

steps.say: How many moles of H₂O actually form when 50.0 mL of 1.20 M HCl meets 50.0 mL of 0.800 M NaOH?
steps.hint: Compute moles of HCl (0.0600 mol) and NaOH (0.0400 mol); the smaller one limits water formed.
steps.explain: HCl is in excess (0.0600 mol), so NaOH limits the reaction to 0.0400 mol H₂O.

steps.say: How much heat is absorbed by the 100.0 g of aqueous solution as it warms from 22.0 °C to 27.1 °C?
steps.hint: Use q_soln = m × c × ΔT with m = 100.0 g and ΔT = 5.1 °C.

steps.say: How much heat is absorbed by the calorimeter itself (C_cal = 25.0 J/°C)?
steps.hint: Use q_cal = C_cal × ΔT.

steps.say: If a student forgot C_cal, how would their calculated |ΔH_rxn| compare to the true value?

options.label: Too small in magnitude, because some heat released went into the cup uncounted
Too large in magnitude, because C_cal subtracts from q_soln
Unchanged, because the cup starts at 22.0 °C
Wrong sign (positive instead of negative)

steps.hint: Total heat released equals q_soln + q_cal; dropping q_cal undercounts heat released.
steps.explain: Omitting C_cal misses the 127.5 J absorbed by the cup, underestimating |ΔH_rxn| by ~6%.

steps.say: What is ΔH_rxn in kJ per mole of H₂O formed? (Include the sign.)
steps.hint: Add q_soln + q_cal, convert J to kJ, make negative (exothermic), and divide by 0.0400 mol.
steps.explain: q_rxn = −(2134 + 127.5) J = −2.261 kJ; dividing by 0.0400 mol gives −56.5 kJ/mol (right near the literature −55.8 kJ/mol).

finish: Every calorimetry error comes from missing a heat sink (the cup) or dividing by the wrong moles (the excess reagent).
takeaway: Write q_rxn = −(q_solution + q_calorimeter) first, and always divide by moles of the limiting reactant.

title: Ice in Warm Water — Boundary Test First
setup: 40.0 g of ice at 0.0 °C is dropped into 100.0 g of liquid water at 25.0 °C in an insulated cup. Given c(water) = 4.184 J/(g·°C) and ΔH_fus = 333.5 J/g, find the final temperature and the mass of ice left unmelted (if any).
strategy: Never assume the final phase before checking the energy budget at the 0 °C phase boundary.

steps.say: What is the maximum heat the 100.0 g of 25.0 °C water can release by cooling all the way down to 0.0 °C?
steps.hint: Use q = m c ΔT for cooling 100.0 g of water by 25.0 °C.

steps.say: How much heat is required to melt all 40.0 g of ice at 0.0 °C?
steps.hint: Multiply 40.0 g by ΔH_fus = 333.5 J/g.
steps.explain: 40.0 g × 333.5 J/g = 13,340 J (13.34 kJ) needed to melt all the ice.

steps.say: Comparing 10,460 J available against 13,340 J needed, what is the final state of the cup?

options.label: An ice-water mixture pinned at exactly 0.0 °C
All liquid water above 0.0 °C
All solid ice below 0.0 °C
Liquid water at 12.5 °C

steps.hint: The warm water runs out of thermal energy at 0 °C before all the ice can melt.
steps.explain: Because 10.46 kJ < 13.34 kJ, melting stops partway through; ice and liquid coexist at 0.0 °C.

steps.say: How many grams of ice melt using the 10,460 J released by the warm water?
steps.hint: Divide the available heat (10,460 J) by ΔH_fus (333.5 J/g).
steps.explain: 10,460 J / 333.5 J/g = 31.36 g of ice melts.

steps.say: How many grams of solid ice remain floating at 0.0 °C?
steps.hint: Subtract the melted ice from the initial 40.0 g of ice.
steps.explain: 40.0 g − 31.36 g = 8.64 g of ice remains at 0.0 °C (and 131.4 g of liquid water).

finish: Had you blindly assumed T_f > 0 °C, the algebra would have returned an unphysical negative temperature — checking the phase boundary first prevents the trap.
takeaway: In any phase-change mixing problem, test the boundary energy (cool to 0 °C vs melt all ice) before writing a final-temperature equation.

title: Back-Titration of an Antacid Tablet
setup: A 0.600 g antacid tablet containing CaCO₃ (M = 100.09 g/mol) and inert binder is dissolved in 50.00 mL of 0.250 M HCl (excess), releasing CO₂. The leftover HCl requires 18.40 mL of 0.150 M NaOH to reach neutralization. Find the mass percent of CaCO₃ in the tablet.
strategy: Treat H⁺ like money in an account: total H⁺ deposited = H⁺ spent on the tablet + H⁺ left over and titrated by NaOH.

steps.say: Why use a back-titration here instead of titrating the CaCO₃ tablet directly with HCl?

options.label: CaCO₃ is insoluble and reacts slowly, so excess HCl dissolves it cleanly and the leftover HCl is easy to titrate
CaCO₃ does not react with HCl unless NaOH is present
NaOH reacts directly with CaCO₃
Back-titration avoids needing the molarity of HCl

steps.hint: Think about trying to spot a sharp endpoint while solid powder is still dissolving.
steps.explain: Solid CaCO₃ dissolves sluggishly near an endpoint; adding excess acid drives full dissolution, and titrating the leftover aqueous HCl gives a sharp endpoint.

steps.say: How many total moles of HCl were originally added to the tablet?
steps.hint: Multiply 0.05000 L by 0.250 mol/L.

steps.say: How many moles of leftover HCl were neutralized by the 18.40 mL of 0.150 M NaOH?
steps.hint: HCl and NaOH react 1:1, so n(HCl leftover) = n(NaOH).
steps.explain: 0.01840 L × 0.150 M = 0.002760 mol leftover HCl.

steps.say: Therefore, how many moles of HCl reacted with the CaCO₃?
steps.hint: Subtract leftover HCl from total HCl added.
steps.explain: 0.01250 − 0.00276 = 0.00974 mol HCl consumed by CaCO₃.

steps.say: From CaCO₃ + 2 HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂, how many moles of CaCO₃ were in the tablet?
steps.hint: Each mole of CaCO₃ consumes 2 moles of HCl.

steps.say: What is the mass percent of CaCO₃ in the 0.600 g tablet?
steps.hint: Multiply moles of CaCO₃ by 100.09 g/mol, divide by 0.600 g, and multiply by 100.

finish: Every back-titration is one subtraction of moles: total reagent added minus excess titrated equals reagent consumed by the unknown.
takeaway: Draw a two-branch mole split for the excess reagent before converting anything to grams.

title: Product-Side Equilibrium via Perfect Square
setup: For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2 HI(g), K_c = 50.0 at 720 K. A rigid flask is charged with 0.500 M HI and no H₂ or I₂. Find [H₂] and [HI] at equilibrium.
strategy: Spot algebraic symmetry (a perfect square) before expanding into a messy quadratic.

steps.say: Starting from pure HI, which direction must the reaction shift, and why?

options.label: Left (toward H₂ and I₂), because Q is infinite while K_c = 50.0
Right (toward HI), because K_c > 1
No shift, because HI is already at 0.500 M
Left only if pressure is lowered

steps.hint: With [H₂] = [I₂] = 0 in the denominator, Q = [HI]² / (0 × 0) → ∞ > K_c.
steps.explain: A reaction with any missing species always shifts to make that species; here Q > K_c drives decomposition of HI.

steps.say: Let x = [H₂] formed at equilibrium. What are [I₂] and [HI] in terms of x?

options.label: [I₂] = x and [HI] = 0.500 − 2x
[I₂] = x and [HI] = 0.500 − x
[I₂] = x and [HI] = 0.500 + 2x

steps.hint: Making 1 mol H₂ and 1 mol I₂ consumes 2 mol HI.
steps.explain: Stoichiometry 1 : 1 : 2 gives [H₂] = x, [I₂] = x, and [HI] = 0.500 − 2x.

steps.say: Substituting into K_c gives (0.500 − 2x)² / x² = 50.0. What is the cleanest first algebra move?

options.label: Take the positive square root of both sides: (0.500 − 2x) / x = √50.0
Assume 2x is negligible compared to 0.500
Expand into 46x² + 2x − 0.25 = 0 and use the quadratic formula
Divide both sides by 0.500

steps.hint: Both numerator and denominator are already squared, and concentrations must be positive.
steps.explain: Taking the positive square root turns the problem into a one-line linear equation with zero approximation.

steps.say: What is [HI] at equilibrium?
steps.hint: Compute 0.500 − 2x.

steps.say: Check your work: what does [HI]² / ([H₂][I₂]) give with 0.390 M and 0.0551 M?
steps.hint: Compute 0.390² / 0.0551².
steps.explain: 0.390² / 0.0551² = 50.1, confirming K_c = 50.0 within rounding.

finish: Spotting the perfect square solves the equilibrium exactly in two lines, and plugging back into K_c proves the numbers cannot be wrong.
takeaway: Look for perfect squares in ICE tables before expanding quadratics, and always substitute your final concentrations back into K as a 5-second proof.

title: Weak Acid + Strong Base Across Three Regimes
setup: 40.0 mL of 0.200 M formic acid, HCOOH (K_a = 1.8 × 10⁻⁴, pK_a = 3.74), is titrated with 0.200 M NaOH. Find the pH after adding (a) 20.0 mL, (b) 40.0 mL, and (c) 45.0 mL of NaOH.
strategy: Always react strong base with weak acid to completion in moles first, account for the new total volume, and then pick the matching equilibrium model.

steps.say: After 20.0 mL of 0.200 M NaOH is added to 40.0 mL of 0.200 M HCOOH, what is the pH without doing any log calculation?
steps.hint: Half of the acid has been converted to conjugate base HCOO⁻, so [HCOO⁻] = [HCOOH].
steps.explain: At half-equivalence, [A⁻] = [HA], so log([A⁻]/[HA]) = 0 and pH = pK_a = 3.74 immediately.

steps.say: At 40.0 mL NaOH (equivalence), all HCOOH has become HCOO⁻. Why is the pH above 7?

options.label: HCOO⁻ is a weak base that takes protons from water, producing OH⁻
Na⁺ makes water basic
Some NaOH is left unreacted at equivalence
Formic acid has pK_a > 7

steps.hint: The only acid-base species left in the beaker at equivalence is the conjugate base HCOO⁻.
steps.explain: At equivalence, stoichiometric neutralization leaves a pure solution of the weak base HCOO⁻.

steps.say: At 40.0 mL NaOH, total volume is 80.0 mL. What is the formal concentration of HCOO⁻ before hydrolysis?
steps.hint: Divide 0.00800 mol HCOO⁻ by the total volume 0.0800 L (don't forget dilution!).
steps.explain: Equal volumes of 0.200 M acid and 0.200 M base double the volume, halving concentration to 0.100 M.

steps.say: Compute K_b for HCOO⁻ using K_w / K_a (K_w = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴, K_a = 1.8 × 10⁻⁴).
steps.hint: Divide 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ by 1.8 × 10⁻⁴.

steps.say: Find the pH at equivalence (40.0 mL NaOH) from [OH⁻] = √(K_b × 0.100).
steps.explain: [OH⁻] = 2.36 × 10⁻⁶ M gives pOH = 5.63 and pH = 8.37.

steps.say: Now at 45.0 mL NaOH (5.0 mL excess NaOH in 85.0 mL total), what is the pH?
steps.hint: Excess OH⁻ = 0.00100 mol in 0.0850 L = 0.01176 M; it completely swamps HCOO⁻ hydrolysis.

finish: One titration spans three completely different chemical regimes — buffer, weak-base salt, and excess strong base — and mole stoichiometry tells you which one you are in.
takeaway: For every acid-base mixture: (1) neutralize in moles, (2) divide by total volume, (3) let the strongest remaining species set the pH.

title: Concentration Cell as a Ratio Meter
setup: A galvanic cell has copper electrodes in both half-cells at 298 K: Cu(s) | Cu²⁺(0.0010 M) || Cu²⁺(1.0 M) | Cu(s). Find which direction electrons flow, the cell voltage, and the [Cu²⁺] ratio needed to generate 0.118 V.
strategy: Use entropy / Le Chatelier to pick the anode before touching Nernst, and treat 0.0592/n as the voltage per decade of concentration ratio.

steps.say: Both half-cells use Cu²⁺/Cu, so E°_cell = 0 V. Which half-cell must be the anode (oxidation) to drive the cell spontaneously?

options.label: The 0.0010 M side, so Cu oxidizes to raise the low [Cu²⁺] while the 1.0 M side plates out
The 1.0 M side, because higher concentration always oxidizes
Neither, because E°_cell = 0 means no current can ever flow
Either side at random

steps.hint: Spontaneous mixing always moves concentrations toward equality.
steps.explain: Equalizing concentrations requires raising [Cu²⁺] on the dilute side (oxidation, anode) and lowering it on the concentrated side (reduction, cathode).

steps.say: For Cu²⁺(conc) + Cu(s) → Cu²⁺(dil) + Cu(s), what is Q = [Cu²⁺]_dil / [Cu²⁺]_conc?
steps.hint: Divide the dilute (product) concentration by the concentrated (reactant) concentration.

steps.say: Using E = E° − (0.0592 / n) log Q with n = 2 at 298 K, what is E_cell?
steps.hint: Each factor of 10 in Q adds 0.0592 / 2 = 0.0296 V, and Q = 10⁻³ is three factors of 10.

steps.say: To boost E_cell from 0.0888 V to 0.1184 V (one more increment of 0.0296 V), what must happen to the ratio [Cu²⁺]_conc / [Cu²⁺]_dil?
steps.hint: 0.1184 / 0.0296 = 4 decades, so the concentration ratio must be 10⁴.
steps.explain: Four increments of 0.0296 V require a 10⁴ (10,000 : 1) concentration ratio.

steps.say: What happens to E_cell as the cell runs for a long time?

options.label: E_cell drops to 0 V when both half-cells reach the same [Cu²⁺]
E_cell stays at 0.0888 V until the copper electrode disappears
E_cell reverses sign halfway through
E_cell rises as [Cu²⁺]_dil increases

steps.hint: When [Cu²⁺]_dil = [Cu²⁺]_conc, Q = 1 and log Q = 0.
steps.explain: When both sides equalize, Q = 1, log Q = 0, and E_cell = 0 V — equilibrium.

finish: Every factor of 10 in concentration ratio shifts a 298 K cell by 59.2/n mV — which is why voltage can measure tiny concentrations.
takeaway: Think of the Nernst term (0.0592/n) log Q as 59.2/n millivolts per power of 10.

title: Pre-Equilibrium Mechanism and Negative Apparent E_a
setup: The reaction 2 NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2 NO₂(g) follows a two-step mechanism: Step 1 (fast equilibrium): 2 NO ⇌ N₂O₂ (K_1 = k_1 / k_{-1}, ΔH_1 = −25 kJ/mol). Step 2 (slow): N₂O₂ + O₂ → 2 NO₂ (rate constant k_2, E_{a,2} = +15 kJ/mol). Derive the rate law and explain why this reaction actually slows down when heated.
strategy: Eliminate the reactive intermediate using the fast equilibrium, then see how K_1(T) and k_2(T) compete when temperature rises.

steps.say: Write the rate of the slow step (Step 2) in terms of the intermediate N₂O₂.

options.label: Rate = k_2 [N₂O₂][O₂]
Rate = k_1 [NO]²
Rate = k_2 [NO₂]²
Rate = k_2 [O₂]

steps.hint: Step 2 is an elementary bimolecular collision between N₂O₂ and O₂.
steps.explain: Elementary step rates use the step's reactants directly: Rate = k_2[N₂O₂][O₂].

steps.say: Using the fast equilibrium K_1 = [N₂O₂] / [NO]², substitute [N₂O₂] into the rate law. What is the overall rate law?

options.label: Rate = k_2 K_1 [NO]²[O₂]
Rate = (k_2 / K_1) [NO]²[O₂]
Rate = k_2 K_1 [NO][O₂]
Rate = k_2 K_1 [NO]²

steps.hint: Solve K_1 = [N₂O₂] / [NO]² for [N₂O₂] = K_1[NO]².
steps.explain: Replacing [N₂O₂] with K_1[NO]² gives Rate = k_obs[NO]²[O₂], where k_obs = k_2 K_1.

steps.say: Step 1 is exothermic (ΔH_1 = −25 kJ/mol). When you raise the temperature, what happens to [N₂O₂] in Step 1?

options.label: K_1 decreases (shifts left), so [N₂O₂] drops
K_1 increases (shifts right), so [N₂O₂] rises
K_1 stays constant because Step 1 is fast
[N₂O₂] doubles every 10 °C

steps.hint: By Le Chatelier's principle, heating an exothermic equilibrium pushes it toward reactants.
steps.explain: Heating breaks apart the weakly bound N₂O₂ dimer, starving Step 2 of its reactant.

steps.say: Because k_obs = K_1 k_2, the apparent activation energy is E_{a,obs} = ΔH_1 + E_{a,2}. Compute E_{a,obs}.
steps.hint: Add ΔH_1 (−25 kJ/mol) and E_{a,2} (+15 kJ/mol).
steps.explain: −25 + 15 = −10 kJ/mol. Losing N₂O₂ hurts the rate more than faster collisions in Step 2 help it.

steps.say: Does a negative apparent E_{a,obs} mean an elementary collision has a negative barrier?

options.label: No — each elementary step has E_a > 0, but k_obs combines k_2 with an exothermic pre-equilibrium K_1
Yes — Step 2 has a negative activation energy
Yes — all third-order reactions have negative barriers
No — it means the reaction is endothermic overall

steps.hint: Both E_{a,1} and E_{a,2} are positive; only the composite sum ΔH_1 + E_{a,2} is negative.
steps.explain: No elementary step has E_a < 0; a negative observed E_a is a classic fingerprint of an exothermic pre-equilibrium.

finish: Composite rate constants hide thermodynamics inside kinetics — whenever a reaction slows down upon heating, suspect an exothermic pre-equilibrium.
takeaway: For a pre-equilibrium mechanism, k_obs = K_1 k_2 implies E_{a,obs} = ΔH_1 + E_{a,2}.

title: Identifying a Metal from Hydrated Oxalate Decomposition
setup: A 1.491 g sample of an unknown hydrated metal(III) oxalate, M₂(C₂O₄)₃·xH₂O, is gently heated to drive off all water, leaving 1.113 g of anhydrous M₂(C₂O₄)₃. Stronger heating decomposes the anhydrous salt completely to 0.357 g of metal oxide M₂O₃ (releasing 3 CO + 3 CO₂ per formula unit). Identify metal M and the hydration number x.
strategy: Find the molar bridge that does NOT depend on the unknown metal M: the mass lost between M₂(C₂O₄)₃ and M₂O₃ is purely 3 CO + 3 CO₂.

steps.say: In M₂(C₂O₄)₃(s) → M₂O₃(s) + 3 CO(g) + 3 CO₂(g), why can we find the moles of salt BEFORE knowing what element M is?

options.label: The mass lost (1.113 − 0.357 g) is entirely 3 CO + 3 CO₂, whose molar mass is known
All trivalent metals have nearly the same atomic mass
M₂O₃ always has molar mass 100 g/mol
Water mass alone determines the metal

steps.hint: Every M atom stays in the solid, so the mass difference between the two solids depends only on C and O.
steps.explain: Because M stays in the crucible, the mass drop from 1.113 g to 0.357 g is purely 3 mol CO + 3 mol CO₂ per mole of salt.

steps.say: What is the combined molar mass of 3 CO + 3 CO₂ lost per mole of M₂(C₂O₄)₃? (C = 12.01, O = 16.00)
steps.hint: CO = 28.01 g/mol and CO₂ = 44.01 g/mol; add 3 of each (or 6 C + 9 O).
steps.explain: 3(28.01) + 3(44.01) = 216.06 g/mol lost per mole of M₂(C₂O₄)₃.

steps.say: How many moles of M₂(C₂O₄)₃ were in the sample?
steps.hint: Divide the mass lost (1.113 − 0.357 = 0.756 g) by 216.06 g/mol.
steps.explain: 0.756 g / 216.06 g/mol = 0.00350 mol of M₂(C₂O₄)₃ (and also 0.00350 mol of M₂O₃).

steps.say: Using the 0.357 g of M₂O₃, what is the molar mass of M₂O₃?
steps.hint: Divide 0.357 g by 0.00350 mol.

steps.say: Subtract 3 O (48.00 g/mol) and divide by 2 to find the atomic mass of M.
steps.hint: (102.0 − 48.00) / 2 gives the atomic mass of M.

steps.say: From the water mass lost in the first heating (1.491 − 1.113 = 0.378 g, M(H₂O) = 18.02 g/mol), find the integer hydration number x.
steps.hint: Find moles of H₂O (0.378 / 18.02 = 0.0210 mol) and divide by moles of salt (0.00350 mol).
steps.explain: 0.0210 / 0.00350 = 6.00, giving Al₂(C₂O₄)₃·6H₂O.

finish: Thermal-gravimetric steps let you peel off known volatile fragments (H₂O, then CO + CO₂) to lock down moles before touching the unknown element.
takeaway: When an element is unknown, look for a mass difference that contains ONLY known elements — that difference immediately gives you moles.

title: Gas Dissociation Equilibrium from Pressure Excess
setup: 2.085 g of PCl₅ (M = 208.24 g/mol) is placed in an evacuated 1.00 L rigid vessel and heated to 500 K, where PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g). The equilibrium total pressure is 0.657 atm. Find the fraction of PCl₅ dissociated (α) and K_p at 500 K.
strategy: Compare the measured pressure against the no-dissociation reference pressure P_0: every mole that dissociates adds 1 net mole of gas, so P_total = P_0(1 + α).

steps.say: What pressure P_0 would 2.085 g of PCl₅ exert in 1.00 L at 500 K if ZERO dissociation occurred? (R = 0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K))
steps.hint: First find n = 2.085 / 208.24 = 0.01001 mol, then P_0 = nRT / V.

steps.say: If a fraction α of PCl₅ dissociates into PCl₃ + Cl₂, how does P_total relate to P_0?

options.label: P_total = P_0 (1 + α)
P_total = P_0 (1 + 2α)
P_total = P_0 (1 − α)
P_total = P_0 (2α)

steps.hint: Start with P_0; lose αP_0 of PCl₅ and gain αP_0 of PCl₃ plus αP_0 of Cl₂.
steps.explain: P_total = P_0(1 − α) + αP_0 + αP_0 = P_0(1 + α). Total pressure ranges from P_0 (α = 0) to 2P_0 (α = 1).

steps.say: From P_total = 0.657 atm and P_0 = 0.4108 atm, find the fraction dissociated α.
steps.hint: Solve α = (P_total / P_0) − 1.

steps.say: What are the equilibrium partial pressures of PCl₃ (and Cl₂) and PCl₅?

options.label: P(PCl₃) = P(Cl₂) = αP_0 = 0.246 atm; P(PCl₅) = (1 − α)P_0 = 0.165 atm
P(PCl₃) = P(Cl₂) = 0.657 / 3 atm; P(PCl₅) = 0.657 / 3 atm
P(PCl₃) = P(Cl₂) = 0.411 atm; P(PCl₅) = 0.246 atm
P(PCl₃) = 0.246 atm; P(Cl₂) = 0.165 atm; P(PCl₅) = 0.246 atm

steps.hint: Check that P(PCl₅) + P(PCl₃) + P(Cl₂) = 0.165 + 0.246 + 0.246 = 0.657 atm.
steps.explain: Each partial pressure scales directly off P_0: αP_0 = 0.246 atm and (1 − α)P_0 = 0.165 atm.

steps.say: Compute K_p = P(PCl₃)·P(Cl₂) / P(PCl₅) at 500 K.

finish: Measuring a single total pressure against the undissociated baseline P_0 determines the entire equilibrium state of a gas reaction.
takeaway: For A(g) ⇌ B(g) + C(g), remember P_total = P_0(1 + α) and K_p = P_0 α² / (1 − α).

title: Normal Boiling Point from Two Vapor Pressures
setup: An unknown liquid has a vapor pressure of 100 mmHg at 300 K and 400 mmHg at 330 K. Estimate its enthalpy of vaporization ΔH_vap and predict its normal boiling point (where P_vap = 760 mmHg). (R = 8.314 J/(mol·K))
strategy: Recognize vapor pressure as an equilibrium constant (K_p = P_vap), apply Clausius–Clapeyron, and bracket the boiling point qualitatively before computing.

steps.say: Jumping from 100 to 400 mmHg (a factor of 4) took +30 K (300 → 330 K). To go from 400 to 760 mmHg (a factor of ~1.9), where should the normal boiling point fall?

options.label: Roughly 345–350 K (about half a 30 K step above 330 K)
Above 380 K, because 360 mmHg is a bigger jump than 300 mmHg
Below 330 K
Exactly 360 K

steps.hint: Vapor pressure grows roughly exponentially with T: equal multiplicative factors (×2) take roughly equal temperature steps (~15 K).
steps.explain: Factor of 4 took 30 K, so a factor of 2 takes ~15 K; 400 → 760 is just under ×2, predicting ~345 K.

steps.say: Compute ln(P₂ / P₁) = ln(400 / 100).
steps.hint: Take the natural log of 4.

steps.say: Using ln(P₂/P₁) = (ΔH_vap / R)(1/T₁ − 1/T₂), find ΔH_vap in kJ/mol.
steps.hint: 1/300 − 1/330 = 3.030 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹; multiply ln(4) by 8.314 and divide by 3.030 × 10⁻⁴, then divide by 1000.

steps.say: Now use P₃ = 760 mmHg and P₂ = 400 mmHg (T₂ = 330 K) to find 1/T_b = 1/330 − (R/ΔH_vap) ln(760/400), and solve for T_b.
steps.explain: T_b = 1 / 0.002890 = 346 K (73 °C) — right inside our 345–350 K estimate!

steps.say: Compute Trouton's ratio ΔS_vap = ΔH_vap / T_b in J/(mol·K). Does it look like a normal non-H-bonding liquid (~85–90) or an H-bonded liquid (~105–110)?
steps.hint: Divide 38,030 J/mol by 346 K.
steps.explain: 38,030 / 346 = 110 J/(mol·K), pointing to strong liquid-phase order such as hydrogen bonding (compare ethanol at 109 J/(mol·K)).

finish: Exponential scaling lets you eyeball boiling points in seconds, and ΔH_vap / T_b even hints at the intermolecular forces inside the liquid.
takeaway: Equal multiplicative jumps in vapor pressure correspond to roughly equal jumps in temperature; Clausius–Clapeyron is van 't Hoff for liquid ⇌ gas.

title: Coupled Equilibria — Dissolving AgCl in Ammonia
setup: AgCl(s) barely dissolves in pure water (K_sp = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰). However, Ag⁺ forms the complex ion [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ with K_f = 1.6 × 10⁷. Find the molar solubility of AgCl in 1.00 M NH₃(aq), and compare it to pure water.
strategy: Add the two reactions to get K_net = K_sp × K_f, then notice the resulting equilibrium expression is a perfect square.

steps.say: First, what is the molar solubility of AgCl in pure water (from s² = K_sp = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰)?
steps.explain: s = √(1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 1.34 × 10⁻⁵ M — barely dissolves.

steps.say: Adding AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ (K_sp) and Ag⁺ + 2 NH₃ ⇌ [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ (K_f) gives AgCl(s) + 2 NH₃ ⇌ [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ + Cl⁻. What is K_net?
steps.hint: When you add two reactions, multiply their equilibrium constants.

steps.say: Because K_f = 1.6 × 10⁷ is huge, almost all dissolved silver sits as [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ rather than free Ag⁺. If s mol/L of AgCl dissolves in 1.00 M NH₃, what is K_net in terms of s?

options.label: K_net = s² / (1.00 − 2s)²
K_net = s² / (1.00 − s)²
K_net = 4s³ / 1.00

steps.hint: Each mole of AgCl dissolved makes 1 mol [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ and 1 mol Cl⁻ while consuming 2 mol NH₃.
steps.explain: Both products equal s and leftover NH₃ is (1.00 − 2s), giving a clean perfect square s² / (1.00 − 2s)² = K_net.

steps.say: Take the square root of both sides: s / (1.00 − 2s) = √(2.88 × 10⁻³). Solve for s.
steps.explain: s = 0.05367 / 1.1073 = 0.0485 M — about 3,600 times more soluble than in pure water!

steps.say: Check our assumption: what is the free [Ag⁺] = K_sp / [Cl⁻] in this solution? (Should be tiny compared to s = 0.0485 M.)
steps.hint: Divide K_sp (1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰) by [Cl⁻] = 0.0485 M.
steps.explain: [Ag⁺] = 3.7 × 10⁻⁹ M, less than 0.00001% of total dissolved silver — confirming our dominant-species assumption.

finish: Coupling a weak solubility equilibrium with a strong complexation equilibrium multiplies K by 10⁷ and turns an insoluble precipitate soluble.
takeaway: In coupled equilibria, combine reactions into one net K, identify the dominant species, and verify at the end that the neglected species is truly tiny.

title: pH of 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ M HCl — Charge Balance Rescue
setup: A student prepares a very dilute strong acid solution: 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ M HCl in pure water at 25 °C (K_w = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴). Find the true pH of this solution.
strategy: When a naive formula gives a physically impossible answer (basic HCl!), fall back to exact conservation laws: charge balance + K_w.

steps.say: If you blindly plug 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ M into pH = −log[HCl], you get pH = 8.0. Why is that impossible?

options.label: Adding an acid to neutral water (pH 7.0) cannot make the solution basic (pH > 7)
HCl is a weak acid at low concentrations
pH can never exceed 7
Water stops autoionizing when HCl is added

steps.hint: Pure water already has 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ M H⁺, ten times more than the HCl you added.
steps.explain: At 10⁻⁸ M, water's own autoionization supplies most of the H⁺; the true pH must sit just barely below 7.00.

steps.say: Every aqueous solution is electrically neutral. Which equation states exact charge balance for HCl in water?
steps.hint: Sum of positive ion charges equals sum of negative ion charges.
steps.explain: Total positive charge [H⁺] must equal total negative charge [Cl⁻] + [OH⁻].

steps.say: Substitute [Cl⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ M and [OH⁻] = K_w / [H⁺]. Multiplying by [H⁺] gives which quadratic?
steps.hint: Move both right-hand terms to the left side of [H⁺]² = (1.0 × 10⁻⁸)[H⁺] + 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴.
steps.explain: [H⁺]² − 10⁻⁸[H⁺] − 10⁻¹⁴ = 0 has one positive root.

steps.say: Solve the quadratic for [H⁺] using the positive root: (10⁻⁸ + √(10⁻¹⁶ + 4 × 10⁻¹⁴)) / 2.
steps.explain: [H⁺] = 1.051 × 10⁻⁷ M (notice water was slightly suppressed from 1.00 × 10⁻⁷ to 0.951 × 10⁻⁷ M by Le Chatelier).

steps.say: What is the true pH of 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ M HCl?
steps.hint: Take −log₁₀(1.051 × 10⁻⁷).
steps.explain: pH = 6.98 — slightly acidic, exactly as physical intuition demanded!

finish: Charge balance never breaks down at any concentration — it seamlessly bridges strong-acid, neutral, and ultra-dilute regimes.
takeaway: When an approximation violates a physical bound (like acid giving pH > 7), write exact charge balance + K_w.

title: Latimer Diagram — Combining Half-Cell Potentials
setup: Standard reduction potentials for iron are: Fe³⁺ + e⁻ → Fe²⁺ (E°₁ = +0.771 V) and Fe²⁺ + 2 e⁻ → Fe (E°₂ = −0.440 V). Find the standard reduction potential E°₃ for the 3-electron reduction Fe³⁺ + 3 e⁻ → Fe, and test whether Fe²⁺ disproportionates into Fe³⁺ and Fe.
strategy: Potentials E° are intensive (J/C) and NEVER add directly; convert to extensive free energy (−nFE°), add, and divide by total electrons.

steps.say: Why can you NOT simply add +0.771 V and −0.440 V to get E° for Fe³⁺ + 3 e⁻ → Fe?

options.label: Voltage is energy per mole of electrons (intensive); only ΔG° = −nFE° (extensive) adds
Iron cannot have a +3 oxidation state in water
Voltages must be multiplied instead of added
The two steps have opposite signs

steps.hint: Step 1 transfers 1 electron while Step 2 transfers 2 electrons — they do not carry equal weight.
steps.explain: Because ΔG°₃ = ΔG°₁ + ΔG°₂, cancelling −F gives n₃E°₃ = n₁E°₁ + n₂E°₂: an electron-weighted average!

steps.say: Compute n₁E°₁ + n₂E°₂ for the two steps (n₁ = 1, n₂ = 2).
steps.explain: 0.771 − 0.880 = −0.109 V (in electron-volt equivalents).

steps.say: Divide by total electrons n₃ = 3 to find E°₃ for Fe³⁺ + 3 e⁻ → Fe.
steps.hint: Divide −0.109 V by 3.
steps.explain: E°₃ = −0.109 / 3 = −0.0363 V (notice how different this is from the naive sum +0.331 V!).

steps.say: Now test disproportionation: 3 Fe²⁺ → 2 Fe³⁺ + Fe. Compute E°_cell = E°(reduction: Fe²⁺/Fe) − E°(oxidation: Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺).
steps.hint: Cathode is Fe²⁺ → Fe (−0.440 V); anode is Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ (use reduction E° = +0.771 V).

steps.say: What does E°_cell = −1.211 V tell you about Fe²⁺ in water, and what happens if you mix Fe³⁺ with solid Fe instead?

options.label: Fe²⁺ is stable against disproportionation; mixing Fe³⁺ + Fe spontaneously comproportionates to Fe²⁺
Fe²⁺ spontaneously decomposes into Fe³⁺ and Fe metal
Neither reaction can occur
Fe³⁺ oxidizes water instead

steps.hint: A negative E°_cell for disproportionation means the reverse reaction (comproportionation) has E° = +1.211 V.
steps.explain: Whenever the potential to the right (−0.44 V) is lower than the potential to the left (+0.77 V) on a Latimer diagram, the middle oxidation state is thermodynamically stable.

finish: Weighting potentials by electron count via ΔG° = −nFE° unlocks every Latimer diagram and lets you spot disproportionation at a glance.
takeaway: For combined half-reactions, use E°_net = (n₁E°₁ + n₂E°₂) / (n₁ + n₂); an intermediate state disproportionates only if E°_right > E°_left.

title: Parallel First-Order Decay and Branching Ratio
setup: An unstable compound A decays simultaneously by two competing first-order pathways: A → B (k₁ = 0.030 s⁻¹) and A → C (k₂ = 0.010 s⁻¹). Starting with [A]₀ = 0.200 M and no B or C, find the effective half-life of A, [A] after 35.0 s, and the final [B] and [C] once all A is gone.
strategy: Competing exit channels add their rate constants (k_eff = k₁ + k₂), and because both pathways share [A] at every instant, the product ratio is locked at k₁ / k₂ forever.

steps.say: With two exit channels open at once (k₁ = 0.030 s⁻¹, k₂ = 0.010 s⁻¹), how does the effective half-life of A compare to path 1 alone?

options.label: Shorter, because k_eff = k₁ + k₂ = 0.040 s⁻¹ drains A faster
Longer, because the two paths interfere with each other
Equal to the average of the two individual half-lives
Controlled only by the slower path k₂

steps.hint: −d[A]/dt = k₁[A] + k₂[A] = (k₁ + k₂)[A]. Opening a second drain empties a tank faster.
steps.explain: Parallel rate constants add directly: k_eff = 0.030 + 0.010 = 0.040 s⁻¹, shortening the half-life.

steps.say: What is the effective half-life t½ of A?
What is [A] after 35.0 s? (Notice 35.0 s is just over two half-lives — eyeball ~0.050 M first!)
steps.explain: 0.200 × e^(−1.40) = 0.0493 M — right beside our two-half-life estimate of 0.050 M.

steps.say: At any moment t, d[B]/dt = k₁[A] and d[C]/dt = k₂[A]. What fraction of consumed A turns into B?
steps.hint: Divide k₁ by (k₁ + k₂).
steps.explain: k₁ / (k₁ + k₂) = 0.030 / 0.040 = 0.75 (75% B, 25% C) at every instant — kinetic control.

steps.say: Once all 0.200 M of A has decayed, what is the final concentration of B?
steps.hint: Multiply [A]₀ (0.200 M) by the branching fraction 0.75.

finish: In parallel pathways, rates add and product yields split strictly in the ratio of rate constants — the foundation of kinetic selectivity.
takeaway: For competing first-order paths: k_eff = k₁ + k₂ (faster decay), and [B]/[C] = k₁/k₂ at every time t.

title: Measuring K_sp of AgI with a Voltmeter
setup: A galvanic cell at 298 K pairs a standard silver cathode, Ag⁺(1.00 M) | Ag(s), with a silver wire dipped into saturated AgI(s) containing 0.100 M I⁻. The voltmeter reads E_cell = +0.888 V. Find [Ag⁺] in the anode and the K_sp of AgI.
strategy: A voltmeter is a logarithmic ion sensor: convert E_cell directly into log[Ag⁺] via the concentration-cell Nernst equation, then multiply by [I⁻] to get K_sp.

steps.say: Why can a voltmeter measure [Ag⁺] ≈ 10⁻¹⁵ M in saturated AgI when no balance or pipette could ever weigh that amount?

options.label: E_cell depends on log[Ag⁺], so every 10× drop in [Ag⁺] adds a clear 0.0592 V
E_cell is directly proportional to [Ag⁺]
I⁻ ions carry the electrons through the wire
AgI dissolves completely when connected to a voltmeter

steps.hint: Check the Nernst equation for a 1-electron concentration cell: E = −0.0592 log[Ag⁺]_anode.
steps.explain: Logarithmic scaling turns 15 orders of magnitude of concentration into an easy-to-read ~0.9 V signal.

steps.say: Both electrodes are Ag(s) (E°_cell = 0, n = 1) and [Ag⁺]_cathode = 1.00 M. From E_cell = −0.0592 log([Ag⁺]_anode / 1.00), what is log₁₀([Ag⁺]_anode)?
steps.hint: Divide −0.888 V by 0.0592 V.

steps.say: Therefore, what is [Ag⁺] in the saturated AgI / 0.100 M I⁻ half-cell?
steps.hint: Raise 10 to the power −15.0.
steps.explain: [Ag⁺]_anode = 10⁻¹⁵.⁰ = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ M.

steps.say: Multiply [Ag⁺] by [I⁻] = 0.100 M to find K_sp of AgI at 298 K.
steps.explain: K_sp(AgI) = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁶ (literature value is 8.5 × 10⁻¹⁷ — right on the mark!).

steps.say: If you increased [I⁻] in the anode from 0.100 M to 1.00 M, how would E_cell change?

options.label: Rise by +0.0592 V (to 0.947 V), because common-ion I⁻ pushes [Ag⁺] down 10×
Drop by 0.0592 V, because more ions reduce resistance
Stay at 0.888 V, because solid AgI is still present
Drop to 0 V

steps.hint: More I⁻ lowers [Ag⁺] by a factor of 10 via K_sp, widening the [Ag⁺] gap between half-cells.
steps.explain: 10× higher [I⁻] forces 10× lower [Ag⁺], adding another +0.0592 V to E_cell.

finish: Electrochemistry and solubility equilibria lock together through [Ag⁺]: a single voltage reading measures K_sp down to 10⁻¹⁶.
takeaway: Whenever a problem pairs a precipitate with a galvanic cell, use Nernst to extract the trace ion concentration, then plug into K_sp.

title: Thermodynamic Coupling in Copper Smelting
setup: Extracting copper directly from Cu₂S(s) → 2 Cu(s) + S(s) is non-spontaneous (ΔG°₁ = +86.2 kJ/mol at 298 K). Burning sulfur, S(s) + O₂(g) → SO₂(g), has ΔG°₂ = −300.1 kJ/mol. Couple these reactions into Cu₂S(s) + O₂(g) → 2 Cu(s) + SO₂(g) to find ΔG°_net, log₁₀ K, and the minimum P(O₂) needed to stay spontaneous when P(SO₂) = 1.0 atm.
strategy: Add ΔG° values to couple a favorable reaction to an unfavorable one, then use ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q = 0 to find the exact pressure threshold.

steps.say: What is ΔG°_net for the coupled smelting reaction Cu₂S(s) + O₂(g) → 2 Cu(s) + SO₂(g)?
steps.hint: Add ΔG°₁ and ΔG°₂; S(s) cancels between the two steps.
steps.explain: +86.2 + (−300.1) = −213.9 kJ/mol — strongly spontaneous.

steps.say: At 298 K, 2.303 RT = 5.708 kJ/mol per power of 10 in K. Roughly what power of 10 is K for ΔG° = −213.9 kJ/mol?
steps.hint: Divide 213.9 kJ/mol by 5.708 kJ/mol to get log₁₀ K.

steps.say: What is the reaction quotient Q for Cu₂S(s) + O₂(g) → 2 Cu(s) + SO₂(g)?

options.label: Q = P(SO₂) / P(O₂)
Q = P(O₂) / P(SO₂)
Q = [Cu]² P(SO₂) / ([Cu₂S] P(O₂))
Q = P(SO₂) · P(O₂)

steps.hint: Pure solids (Cu₂S, Cu) have activity 1 and drop out of Q.
steps.explain: Only the two gases enter Q: Q = P(SO₂) / P(O₂).

steps.say: The reaction stops being spontaneous when Q = K (so ΔG = 0). If P(SO₂) = 1.0 atm, what is the minimum P(O₂) = 1.0 / K?
steps.explain: Even a single molecule of O₂ in a room exceeds 10⁻³⁸ atm — thermodynamically, smelting runs to completion.

steps.say: If ΔG° is −213.9 kJ/mol at 298 K, why doesn't copper sulfide ore spontaneously turn into copper metal on a shelf at room temperature?

options.label: High activation energy (kinetics): the reaction is thermodynamically favored but immeasurably slow at 298 K
Air does not contain enough O₂
ΔG° is positive at room temperature
Cu₂S cannot react with O₂ at any temperature

steps.hint: Distinguish thermodynamics (whether a reaction is favored) from kinetics (how fast it happens).
steps.explain: Thermodynamics says 'yes' (K ~ 10³⁷), but solid-state diffusion and bond breaking have a huge activation barrier — hence a furnace is needed for speed, not spontaneity.

finish: Remembering 5.71 kJ/mol per decade of K at 298 K lets you jump instantaneously between free energy, equilibrium constants, and pressure thresholds.
takeaway: At 298 K, every −5.71 kJ/mol of ΔG° multiplies K by 10 — and always separate thermodynamic favorability from kinetic speed.

title: Identifying a Diprotic Acid by Titration and Gas Volume
setup: A 0.450 g sample of an unknown solid diprotic acid, H₂A, is completely neutralized by 25.00 mL of 0.400 M NaOH. A second identical 0.450 g sample reacts with excess NaHCO₃(aq), releasing CO₂(g) into an evacuated 0.250 L rigid flask at 298 K. Find the molar mass of H₂A and the pressure of CO₂ produced.
strategy: Use proton equivalents (H⁺) as the single conserved currency linking titration, molar mass, and gas pressure.

steps.say: How many moles of H⁺ did the 0.450 g sample of H₂A supply to the 25.00 mL of 0.400 M NaOH?
steps.hint: Every mole of OH⁻ neutralizes one mole of H⁺.

steps.say: Because H₂A is diprotic (2 H⁺ per molecule), how many moles of H₂A are in 0.450 g?
steps.hint: Divide moles of H⁺ by 2.

steps.say: What is the molar mass of the unknown diprotic acid H₂A?
steps.hint: Divide 0.450 g by 0.00500 mol.
steps.explain: 0.450 / 0.00500 = 90.0 g/mol — matching anhydrous oxalic acid, H₂C₂O₄ (90.03 g/mol)!

steps.say: Each H⁺ reacts with HCO₃⁻ via H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ → H₂O + CO₂(g). How many moles of CO₂ form from the second 0.450 g sample?
steps.hint: One mole of H⁺ produces one mole of CO₂ — so you don't even need the molar mass to know n(CO₂)!
steps.explain: Both protons react with excess HCO₃⁻, so n(CO₂) = n(H⁺) = 0.0100 mol.

steps.say: What pressure does 0.0100 mol CO₂ exert in 0.250 L at 298 K? (R = 0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K))
steps.hint: Use P = nRT / V with n = 0.0100 mol, T = 298 K, V = 0.250 L.

finish: Tracking proton equivalents links titration volume directly to gas pressure and molar mass without extra detours.
takeaway: In acid-base and carbonate problems, count moles of H⁺ directly — it is the invariant bridge across reactions.

title: Manganese in Steel by Redox Oxidation and Absorbance
setup: A 0.500 g steel alloy sample is dissolved in acid, converting all manganese to Mn²⁺. Periodate oxidizes all Mn²⁺ quantitatively to purple MnO₄⁻, and the solution is diluted to 250.0 mL. In a 1.00 cm cuvette at 525 nm (ε = 2400 M⁻¹·cm⁻¹), the absorbance is A = 0.432. Find the oxidation-state electron transfer and the mass percent of Mn (M = 54.94 g/mol) in the steel.
strategy: Chain Mn atom conservation backward from light absorbance in the cuvette to the original steel alloy.

steps.say: How many electrons are lost per Mn atom when Mn²⁺ is oxidized to MnO₄⁻?
steps.hint: In MnO₄⁻, four O atoms are −2 each (−8 total) and the ion charge is −1, so Mn is +7.
steps.explain: Mn goes from +2 to +7, losing 5 electrons per Mn atom.

steps.say: From A = εbc (A = 0.432, ε = 2400 M⁻¹·cm⁻¹, b = 1.00 cm), what is [MnO₄⁻] in the 250.0 mL flask?
steps.hint: Divide A by εb: 0.432 / 2400.

steps.say: How many moles of Mn were in the 250.0 mL flask (and therefore in the 0.500 g steel sample)?
steps.hint: Multiply [MnO₄⁻] by 0.2500 L; Mn is conserved 1:1 from alloy to Mn²⁺ to MnO₄⁻.

steps.say: Convert 4.50 × 10⁻⁵ mol Mn (M = 54.94 g/mol) to milligrams of Mn.
steps.hint: Multiply moles by 54.94 g/mol to get grams, then × 1000 for mg.

steps.say: What is the mass percent of Mn in the 0.500 g (500 mg) steel sample?
steps.hint: Divide 2.472 mg by 500 mg and multiply by 100.
steps.explain: 2.472 / 500 × 100 = 0.494% Mn — typical for carbon steel (0.3–1.0% Mn).

finish: Turning a trace metal into a strongly absorbing species (MnO₄⁻) lets spectrophotometry measure sub-percent alloy composition accurately.
takeaway: In multi-step analytical chains (dissolve → oxidize → dilute → measure A), trace the conserved atom (1 Mn → 1 Mn²⁺ → 1 MnO₄⁻) straight back to the sample.
